analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federal construction contractors to pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act died in committee without a hearing or a vote, with 4 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires companies on federally funded construction projects to pay workers the wage that is standard for their trade and area, and to keep payroll records. This bill would repeal that requirement entirely, 30 days after it was enacted, while leaving existing contracts untouched. It would let federal contractors set their own pay on public projects. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal construction contractors and firms bidding on government-funded building projects, who could hire workers at below the local prevailing rate and lower their bids as a result. Taxpayers would see lower bids only if contractors passed savings through rather than keeping them.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40, the Davis-Bacon Act, removing the requirement that workers on federally financed construction be paid the locally prevailing wage [S3].
Declares null and void any reference in any other law to a Davis-Bacon wage requirement, wiping out prevailing-wage standards in related statutes [S2].
Takes effect 30 days after enactment but does not affect contracts already in existence or bids already outstanding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction laborers and mechanics on federal projects, who could be paid less than the local standard for their trade, and in practice the organized building-trades unions that rely on prevailing-wage rules to hold wages up. The lower-quality work and safety record associated with lower wages would fall on the communities using the public buildings.

drawbacks.text: Removing the prevailing-wage floor lets contractors cut labor costs on public projects by paying below the local standard, directly lowering the pay of construction workers the federal government pays for [S2].
Repeal also erases prevailing-wage requirements written into other federal laws, since the bill voids all references to Davis-Bacon wage requirements across the code [S2].

The Act also requires payroll certifications, which are a main tool for detecting wage theft and misclassification on public jobs; repealing the Act removes those reporting requirements along with the wage floor (mechanism of the Act as summarized by CRS) [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main argument for repeal is that prevailing-wage rules raise the cost of federally funded construction. The cost falls on a specific group: workers on those projects, who lose the local wage standard for their trade, and the payroll records that let the government catch underpayment. Supporters of the wage floor argue repeal mostly shifts money from workers' paychecks to contractors' margins rather than to taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King introduced the bill on May 16, 2013, joined by Rep. Jason Chaffetz, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S5].
On July 8, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it stayed for the rest of the 113th Congress with no further action [S5].
It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House or Senate [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers and building-trades unions kept the prevailing-wage floor on federal projects, since repeal never advanced; contractors who wanted to shed the wage requirement gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers kept the wage floor

for.name: Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and took no further action to move it beyond committee referral.

for.name: Jason Chaffetz
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the repeal.

for.name: 3 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none took further action to advance it.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Kline (R-MN)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup, and its subcommittee on Workforce Protections never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and cosponsorship was Republican: the sponsor and 3 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support listed.

industries.note: Repeal would have let contractors bid for federally funded work without paying the local prevailing wage, cutting their labor costs on public projects. The savings to bidders would come out of construction workers' pay, not necessarily out of the government's bill.

industries.industry: Building-trades unions and organized construction labor
industries.note: Davis-Bacon's prevailing-wage standard is the main federal lever that unions and open-shop workers alike use to hold pay at local trade rates on government projects; repeal would remove it. Their interest here runs with the workers themselves.
